newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Palestinian film records Jewish settler ire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Palestinian film records Jewish settler ire.

text.p: Palestinian film director Mohammed Sawalmeh said he was stunned when he got a peek inside the fortified Jewish settlements of the West Bank.
For six months he criss-crossed the West Bank with an Israeli television crew, asking settlers their views of Palestinians and the prospects for coexistence.
Sawalmeh, who has spent most of his 42 years in other Arab countries and Russia, said none of the 27 settlers he interviewed had a good word to say about Palestinians.

The 52-minute documentary, produced for the Palestinian Ministry of Information and unveiled at the Arab Television Festival in Cairo, aims to uncover how the 130,000 Jewish settlers relate to the one million Arabs in the West Bank.
The film is called "The Coming Fire".

"I chose this title for my film after what I saw and heard from the settlers. The issue of settlements is a very dangerous phenomenon which I think, unless a solution is found, will ignite the whole peace process," Sawalmeh told Reuters.
"I hoped to meet at least one who would tell me that he was ready to live together in peace with Arabs. But I did not find any," he complained.
DIRECTOR ASTONISHED BY DEPTH OF HATRED

Sawalmeh grew up in exile. His family fled the West Bank after Israel occupied his homeland in the 1967 Middle East war. He said he was astonished to the point of fear by the depth of hatred shown by settlers towards Arabs.

The film maker, who returned to the West Bank in 1994 after Israel and the PLO signed their self-rule deal, said he omitted much of the obscene language and harsh verbal attacks recorded in the 30 hours of taped material he collected.

He hired a helicopter to take aerial shots of some 140 fenced-off and fortified enclaves across the West Bank. The film shows a West Bank landscape dotted with mostly red-roofed Jewish settlements on hilltops.
Sawalmeh spoke to some of the settlers in Russian, a language he mastered while studying film making in the former Soviet Union.

On one occasion, he said he was Russian to protect himself and his crew from being assaulted should settlers find out he was a Palestinian. He said he told one settler he was from the Russia's Caucasus region, an area where people have dark skin like his.
"I often heard that settlers were extremists. But it is different when you encounter them face to face," he recalled.
Sawalmeh said he and a Palestinian crew were assaulted three times by settlers while filming in and near Arab villages adjacent to settlements.
HAWKISH SETTLERS, HOSTILE VIEWS
Some of the 15 Palestinians interviewed for the film complain about Jews seizing the West Bank land captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
The film does not delve into the traditional religious, nationalist and economic reasons that settlers give for making their homes in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"Settlers assert a religious supremacy to explain why they settle in the West Bank," says the movie's narrator.
In one interview after another, settlers spell out their feelings towards Arabs and their vision of the future.

"Arabs must restore to us south Lebanon, Damascus, Jordan and Sinai so we would accept to make peace with them," says one red-bearded settler in his 40s, referring to the lands of neighbouring countries.

An elderly settler wearing a black coat discounts the possibility of reaching peace with the Palestinians, calling his Arab neighbours "riff-raff who are only capable of stealing and carrying out massacres".
Settlers in the West Bank town of Hebron -- revered by both Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the patriarch Abraham -- appear to reflect more hawkish views than others.
One restaurant owner, shown making a beef sandwich for a customer, is asked about the prospects of living together in peace with Palestinians.
"Coexistence," the settler snaps in surprise. "We have to kick the Arabs out of Israel and I am not saying to drive them out but to kick them out without any compensation. They are murderers."

One of his customers suggests to the camera crew that they visit the grave of settler Baruch Goldstein, who in 1994 killed 29 Moslem worshippers kneeling in prayer at Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, before survivors beat him to death.
"Have you visited the grave of the saint?" the settler says, referring to Goldstein. "I wish there were 10,000 people like him."
